newsitem.title: UK: Weak RPI data cool UK rate fears but M4 niggles.
newsitem.headline: Weak RPI data cool UK rate fears but M4 niggles.

text.p: A slight fall in underlying UK retail prices in February has calmed fears UK interest rates may need to rise sharply to contain inflationary pressures.
But a surge in the broad money supply measure M4, together with strong labour market and sales data on Wednesday, means the concerns have not been wholly laid to rest.

"Overall today's figures are slightly helpful on interest rates but set against yesterday's, my guess is still that the post election rise is 50 basis points," Salomon Brothers economist Michael Saunders said.

The UK faces an election on May 1 and the ruling Conservative Party -- already more than 20 points behind in the opinion polls -- is not expected to risk further unpopularity by increasing the country's 6.0 percent interest rates before the vote despite Bank of England requests for higher rates.
Today's M4 data which showed a leap in the annual seasonally adjusted rate to 11.3 percent in February from a revised 10.0 percent in January has bolstered the Bank's case.
"The strong money supply data will be seized on by the Bank of England to sustain its campaign for higher rates," CIBC chief economist David Coleman said.
The M4 data have been distorted by the introduction of the gilt repo but analysts say the strong growth rate still tallies with a picture of corporate and consumer confidence.
But the retail price data at least went Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's way.
UK underlying retail prices rose by an annual underlying 2.9 percent in February, down from 3.1 percent in January but still above the official target of 2.5 percent.
The headline rate dipped to a lower than expected 2.7 percent year on year.

"If anything the numbers are slightly better than the market was looking for. They will take some of the heat off the Chancellor after the very strong figures we saw yesterday," GNI economist Peter Osler said.

Analysts said that an unexpectedly large drop in seasonal food prices was one of the main reasons for the slowdown in overall retail price inflation but they were encouraged by the fact that non-seasonal food prices also fell, suggesting supermarket price wars were continuing.
"The forces which will bring inflation down sharply in 1997 are increasingly evident," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes. "Mr. Clarke's target of 2.5 percent or less is back in sight."
But other analysts were less sanguine. "I think the chances of hitting the target are close to zero," said Co-operative Bank Treasury economist Andrew Snowball.
"We're seeing the temporary effects of the strength of sterling and some residual resistance from consumers to price rises," he said.

Other inflation hawks also warn that growth in average earnings, falling unemployment, tax cuts which kick in in April and windfall payments from building society mergers form a recipe for another consumer boom.
Snowball expects UK interest rates to be close to 6.75 percent by the end of the year as the new government tries to put inflation back under the leash.
But he is one of a growing band which advocates using a fiscal policy tightening so that rates do not have to go up too far.
Putting up interest rates hits the vulnerable British manufacturing sector as well as the buoyant consumer and service sectors.
